metaDescription: Six Hoshizaki commercial ice machines compared: top hat and crescent undercounter models, a cubelet dispenser and a modular head, with AHRI output explained.
expertTake: The Hoshizaki KM-231BAJ with an 80 lb bin is the all-round pick for a busy bar or cafe, since its AHRI certified output matches the storage behind it. The AM-50BAK is the right choice when the space is tight and the demand is modest. Skip the nominal output figures when you compare machines, because the AHRI numbers at warm water and warm air are the ones you will actually live with.
introParagraphs: One Japanese maker builds commercial ice machines for kitchens, bars and care facilities, and its line is organized around three questions: what shape of ice, how much of it and where it is stored. Some machines include a bin under the evaporator, and others are modular heads that sit on a bin you buy separately.

The numbers on a commercial spec sheet are quoted at two sets of conditions, a cool test and a warm one, and the gap between them is often thirty percent or more. We rank the machines by the output you can rely on in a real kitchen, the storage behind it and the footprint and service life each model brings.

products.name: Hoshizaki KM-231BAJ crescent cuber with 80 lb bin, air-cooled, 24 in

specList.label: Nominal output
specList.value: Up to 213 lb per 24 hours at 70/50

products.description:
This KM-231BAJ pairs an air-cooled crescent cuber with an 80 pound built-in bin in a 24 inch cabinet, which is the right size for a bar, a cafe or a small restaurant. The spec sheet states nominal output up to 213 pounds per 24 hours under cool conditions and 147 pounds at the warm AHRI test, and the second number is the one to plan around.

Crescent cubes are the familiar half-moon shape that restaurants use, and the front-opening bin, stainless exterior and 6 inch painted legs suit a working kitchen. The self-contained condenser means no remote compressor and no water-cooled loop. The balance between 147 pounds of dependable output and an 80 pound reserve is why it leads this guide.

Compared with the 17.75 inch KM-81BAJ it makes nearly three times as much and stores twice the ice. Clean the condenser, sanitize the bin on a schedule and descale the water system.
products.bestFor: Busy bars, cafes and small restaurants.
pros: 147 lb AHRI output with an 80 lb bin
cons: 24 inch width needs real floor space
Needs a plumbed water line and drain

products.name: Hoshizaki AM-50BAK air-cooled top hat ice machine with 27 lb bin

specList.label: Warranty
specList.value: 2 years parts and labor on the machine

products.description:
At 14-7/8 inches wide the AM-50BAK is one of the narrowest commercial ice machines you can buy, and it still makes up to 54 pounds in 24 hours into a 27 pound built-in bin. The top hat cube is a clear, full-bodied piece that melts slowly and suits a premium drink.

The maker lists a two-year parts and labor warranty on the whole machine and describes clean ice and easy maintenance that support a longer unit life. That warranty is a real selling point in a commercial purchase, where the compressor and the control board are the costly parts. The narrow cabinet makes it a fit for a bar back, a small office or a restaurant with a tight kitchen.

Compared with the KM-231BAJ it makes a quarter of the ice in a quarter of the width. Sanitize the bin monthly, brush the condenser and descale the water system.
products.bestFor: Small bars and offices that need a narrow, clear-cube machine.
pros: Top hat clear cubes melt slowly
cons: 54 lb per 24 hours limits heavy use
Small bin for a busy hour

products.name: Hoshizaki KM-81BAJ undercounter crescent cuber, 38 lb bin, 17.75 in

specList.label: Nominal output
specList.value: Up to 78 lb per 24 hours at 70/50

products.description:
The KM-81BAJ is the middle step between the narrow AM-50BAK and the 24 inch KM-231BAJ: an air-cooled undercounter crescent cuber with a 38 pound bin in a 17.75 inch cabinet. Nominal output reaches 78 pounds per 24 hours, but the AHRI figure at warm conditions is 52 pounds, a gap that buyers should read carefully.

The front-opening bin, stainless steel exterior and 6 inch painted legs suit a working kitchen. Crescent cubes pour well and fill a glass efficiently. It suits a cafe, a small bar or a break room that needs more than a gourmet machine's reserve.

Compared with the AM-50BAK it makes more and stores more at a higher price and a wider cabinet. Keep the air inlet clear, sanitize the bin on a schedule and descale regularly.
products.bestFor: Cafes and small bars wanting a mid-size undercounter cuber.
pros: Crescent cubes pour and fill well
cons: 52 lb AHRI output is well below the 78 lb nominal

products.name: Hoshizaki KM-301BAJ 30 in crescent cuber with 100 lb bin, air-cooled

specList.label: Nominal output
specList.value: Up to 290 lb per 24 hours at 70/50

products.description:
The KM-301BAJ steps up to a 30 inch cabinet with a 100 pound built-in bin and an AHRI output of 212 pounds, well above the 24 inch KM-231BAJ. It is aimed at a restaurant or a busy bar that burns through ice at peak hours and needs a reserve.

The nominal 290 pounds at cool conditions is the headline, and the 212 pound AHRI figure is the sober number. The air-cooled self-contained condenser keeps installation simple, and the front-opening bin and stainless exterior match the rest of the range.

Compared with the KM-231BAJ it makes about 45 percent more by the AHRI figure and holds 20 more pounds. Clean the condenser monthly, sanitize the bin and descale the water system.
products.bestFor: Restaurants and bars with heavy peak-hour demand.
cons: Needs a plumbed water line and drain

products.name: Hoshizaki DCM-271BAK cubelet machine with water dispenser, 10 lb bin
products.description:
A cubelet machine makes small, soft, chewable pieces, the commercial cousin of nugget ice, and the DCM-271BAK adds a water dispenser. It produces up to 286 pounds in 24 hours, a very high rate for its 16-5/8 inch width, but its built-in bin holds only about 10 pounds.

That storage figure is the clue to how it works: it is a dispensing machine for a place that serves ice and water constantly, like a care home, a hospital or a self-serve counter, where ice is made on demand and handed out. It is not a reserve machine. Chewable cubelets are popular where patients or customers prefer soft ice.

Compared with the crescent cubers it makes a different ice and stores far less. Clean the dispenser, sanitize the bin and descale the water system on a schedule.
products.bestFor: Care homes, hospitals and self-serve counters wanting soft ice and water.
pros: Up to 286 lb per 24 hours in a narrow cabinet
cons: Only about 10 lb of built-in storage

products.name: Hoshizaki KM-350MAJ 22 in modular crescent ice machine, 489 lb nominal

specList.label: Nominal output
specList.value: Up to 489 lb per 24 hours at 70/50

products.description:
The KM-350MAJ is a modular head, which means it makes ice but does not include a bin; you place it on a bin sized to your needs. It is a 22 inch machine with a nominal 489 pound output and a 393 pound AHRI figure, the highest in this guide, drawing 9.05 amps on a 115 volt supply.

That modular approach is the point. A restaurant that needs a large reserve can set the head on a big bin, while a bar can choose a smaller one, so the machine and the storage scale independently. It carries NSF, UL and ENERGY STAR listings and uses R-404A refrigerant in a self-contained air-cooled design.

Compared with the bin-equipped models it needs a separate bin purchase and more planning. Keep the condenser clean, sanitize the bin below and descale the water system.
products.bestFor: High-volume kitchens that want to size the bin separately.
pros: 393 lb AHRI output is the highest here
Modular head pairs with any bin
NSF, UL and ENERGY STAR listed
cons: Needs careful planning for plumbing and space

buyingCriteria.explanation: Hoshizaki quotes output at two conditions. The KM-81BAJ lists up to 78 pounds at a cool 70 degree air and 50 degree water test but only 52 pounds AHRI at 90 degree air and 70 degree water, while the KM-301BAJ lists 290 and 212. A hot kitchen behaves like the warm test, so plan around the AHRI figure. Treat the nominal output as a laboratory best case.

A machine's daily output is useless if the bin cannot hold the rush. The KM-231BAJ pairs 147 pounds AHRI with an 80 pound bin, the KM-301BAJ pairs 212 with 100 pounds, and the DCM-271BAK pairs 286 with only about 10. Estimate your peak hour, then match the bin.

Crescent cubes in the KM models are standard restaurant ice, top hat cubes in the AM models are clear and slow melting for premium drinks, and cubelets in the DCM are soft and chewable. The shape changes how fast a drink chills and how it dilutes. Choose the shape for the drink, not for the spec sheet.

The AM-50BAK is 14-7/8 inches wide, the KM-81BAJ 17.75 inches, the KM-231BAJ 24 inches and the KM-301BAJ 30 inches. Front in, front out airflow on some models removes the need for side and rear clearance, which helps in built-in spots. Measure the space and the airflow path before you buy. An air-cooled machine in a closet with no ventilation will pull in its own hot exhaust, and a machine that runs hot makes less ice and wears faster.

The KM-350MAJ is a head without a bin, which lets you pick a bin size and swap it later. The other models include a bin, which is simpler and cheaper. Choose modular if demand is large or may grow, and built-in if you want one box and a quick install.

The AM-50BAK lists a two-year parts and labor warranty on the whole machine, which is a strong statement in a commercial purchase. A commercial machine lives on cleaning and service, so confirm the warranty terms and find a service company before you install.

howWeEvaluated.title: Realistic output
howWeEvaluated.description: We favored AHRI figures at warm conditions over nominal numbers, such as 147 lb on the KM-231BAJ against 213 nominal. A hot kitchen behaves like the warm test. We noted the percentage gap on each model.

howWeEvaluated.title: Storage match
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared bin sizes, from 10 to 100 pounds, against the AHRI output. A balanced pairing scored best. A high output with a tiny bin was reserved for dispensing uses.

howWeEvaluated.title: Ice type fit
howWeEvaluated.description: We separated crescent, top hat and cubelet machines by use. A bar, a cafe and a care home want different ice. We did not rank across shapes.

howWeEvaluated.title: Footprint and airflow
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at widths from 14-7/8 to 30 inches and at front airflow designs. Narrow machines scored for tight spaces. Large machines were flagged for floor space.

howWeEvaluated.title: Service and support
howWeEvaluated.description: We considered the AM-50BAK's two-year parts and labor warranty, NSF and UL listings and brand reputation in commercial kitchens. A commercial machine depends on service, so support counted.

cards.text: The KM-350MAJ makes ice and sits on a bin you select, letting you scale storage separately.

cards.text: A narrow cabinet, front in and front out airflow and a bin sized to your peak.

maintenance.why: Dust and grease block heat rejection and cut AHRI output. A brush or vacuum keeps it near spec, and a kitchen with fryers nearby may need the coil cleaned every couple of weeks, with the machine switched off and unplugged first.
A warm, wet bin grows slime. Use an approved sanitizer and rinse well.
Scale coats the evaporator and cuts output. Use a maker-approved descaler and rinse thoroughly.
A spent filter restricts the water supply and lets scale-forming minerals reach the evaporator. Keep a spare on hand.
A blocked drain floods the bin or the floor. Pour water through to confirm flow.

faq.a: It is the daily output measured at 90 degree air and 70 degree water, a warm-kitchen test. It is lower than the nominal figure measured at 70 and 50, and it is the one to plan around. The gap can be a third or more, as the KM-81BAJ shows with 78 nominal against 52 AHRI, so a machine chosen on the nominal number can fall short on a hot day.

faq.q: Which Hoshizaki is best for a small bar?
faq.a: The AM-50BAK for tight space and modest demand, or the KM-81BAJ for a bit more ice. Larger bars suit the KM-231BAJ. Think about the bin as much as the machine: a bar that pours a lot of drinks in one hour wants a reserve in the bin, not just a high daily rating, and the 38 and 80 pound bins here are the figures to compare.

It makes small, soft, chewable ice pieces, the commercial cousin of nugget ice. The DCM-271BAK adds a water dispenser and a small bin. It suits places where ice is handed out all day, such as care settings, because the machine makes ice as it is used, and it is the wrong choice for a bar that needs a large reserve.

faq.q: Do I need a separate bin?
faq.a: Only for the modular KM-350MAJ. The other models in this guide include a built-in bin.

faq.q: Do these machines need a drain?
faq.a: Yes. Commercial ice machines need a water line and a drain, and a drain pump helps when the drain is higher than the machine. Plan the plumbing before you buy, because a drain run to a floor sink or a standpipe is often the biggest installation cost and a code requirement in many places.

faq.q: How long should a commercial ice machine last?
faq.a: Many serve for years with regular cleaning and descaling. Neglect shortens that far more than heavy use does. The usual failures are water side: scale on the evaporator and slime in the bin, so a filter, a descale calendar and a trained staff member matter more than any option on the spec sheet.
